**Response to Reviewer Pm4m**

We thank the reviewer for the detailed, fair reading, and for noting that concerns, once addressed, would raise the score. We answer every point. All supporting results are already in the submitted paper unless tagged [NEW]; because the PDF is frozen, presentation fixes are stated as camera-ready commitments ("we will...").

**W1 (framing / DLinear).** This is the central point and we treat it as such, but one correction changes the conclusion. We appreciate the reviewer holding the method to a from-scratch DLinear, and the observation is exactly right for RR-MoA-proper, the minimal diagnostic probe whose only role is to isolate the router input. We would gently add that it does not carry over to the method we deploy: Residual-IA+, reported in the submitted Appendix P, matches or beats DLinear rather than trailing it:
- 65 significant wins vs 11 losses (5.9:1); 107/123 match-or-beat (87%) across 6 backbones × 6 datasets × 4 horizons.
- 6/6 at the H=192 deployment horizon; MOMENT-large 23/24 with zero losses (16 significant wins); Moirai-MoE 15/15 (100%).
- It dominates on non-stationary data at long horizons (ETTm2 -27.0% at H=720; ETTh2 wins at all four horizons).
- Even at the single least-favorable slice cited (MOMENT-small, H=96), the net mean gap is -2.8%, a win, with ETTh1 the only loss.

We read the criticism as fair about our framing, not our evidence: we led with "5/6 match-or-beat" and titled the appendix "Closing the DLinear Gap," which foregrounded the one losing cell (ETTh1/H=96). We will (i) promote the full grid and the 65:11 win-count into the main text, (ii) retitle to the outperformance the numbers show, and (iii) reframe the abstract's DLinear comparison as scope, not deficit: "Because the router isolates the collapse mechanism rather than maximizing accuracy, the minimal RR-MoA probe trails a from-scratch DLinear on linear-dominated datasets; our deployment adapter Residual-IA+ removes this gap, matching or beating DLinear across six backbones and four horizons." We also accept the narrow, true version: RR-MoA-proper does trail DLinear in absolute MSE, sharpest on ETTh1/H=96, and we will introduce it plainly as a diagnostic instrument, not an accuracy claim.

**W2 (Figure 2).** Agreed. We will redraw Figure 2 at larger size with non-overlapping modules and a clearer depiction of the raw-router and frozen-expert paths.

**W3 (Moirai gains without collapse).** A fair distinction. Moirai applies non-learnable instance normalization (Kim et al. 2022, i.e. RevIN) to inputs/outputs, stripping the same per-window location-scale we study, minus the learnable affine. Raw routing recovers the stripped signal there by the same input-side mechanism, while the absence of learnable affine is exactly why AdaMix does not collapse on Moirai: the sudden collapse is driven by gradient co-adaptation and requires a learnable affine. The unified claim is "raw routing helps whenever per-window statistics are stripped from the router's input," and collapse is the severe failure mode that additionally requires learnable affine. We will present the cross-backbone results as consistent with the diagnosis rather than as uniform collapse-repair, and add the Moirai citation.

**W4 (heavy tuning; generalization beyond six).** On "heavy tuning": the 546-run sweep was development effort, and we agree it should not be presented as a SOTA search. We would add that the endpoint is not merely parity with DLinear but a win (65:11), and that the recipe is fixed rather than per-dataset tuned. [NEW] Applied unchanged (gate-init b=-2, 5-epoch warmup, shared NLinear, validation early-stop) to three datasets it had never seen, Residual-IA+ matches or beats DLinear on 8/9 (dataset, seed) cells: Solar 3/3 (-9.5%), Traffic 3/3 (parity), Exchange 2/3, no collapse. A recipe that transfers to unseen data without re-tuning speaks against the dataset-specific-engineering reading, and directly addresses "generalization beyond these six is unclear."

On "the raw branch does the work; the TSFM is dead weight (P.3)": one clarification we should have made explicit. P.3's "dead weight" verdict is measured against the intermediate Dual-Stream (ETTh2 0.452, ETTm2 0.252), not the final Residual-IA+ (ETTh2 0.346, ETTm2 0.188), and that intermediate architecture itself loses to DLinear. P.3's own backbone-free Raw-MLP MoE loses to DLinear by +11.2% on all six datasets: remove the TSFM and you fall behind DLinear; it is the TSFM-inclusive Residual-IA+ that gets ahead. [NEW] We ran the clean isolation directly, Residual-IA+ vs an identical-budget backbone-free Raw-MLP MoE, holding the raw branch fixed and toggling only the backbone, at H=192 (where the paper reports the backbone contributes maximally): Residual-IA+ wins 18/18 (mean -11.8%), including ETTh2/ETTm2/Electricity, the very datasets flagged as dead-weight at H=96, while still matching or beating a 49K DLinear. The backbone's contribution is therefore horizon-dependent: small at H=96 on linear-dominated data, decisively positive at H≥192.

**W5 ((μ,σ) tension).** The tension is real, and re-scoping Observation 1 resolves it: R(D) is the ratio of routing-discriminative variance in the instance-norm-removable component (location-scale) to that in the surviving component (shape), not a claim that (μ,σ) is the whole routing signal. When the ratio is high, stripping (μ,σ) removes most of the routing signal and routing collapses; when it is low (Traffic, R=0.14) the signal lives in the surviving shape, so stripping does not hurt and RR-MoA correctly does not improve. This is exactly consistent with the ablations cited: [μ,σ]-only routing degrades +48% (SSR) and temporal shuffling moves performance ≤3%. We will re-scope Observation 1 explicitly as a vulnerability predictor / lower bound, not a sufficiency claim.

**W6 (minor).** All accepted. The router parameter count is 853 (Conv1d 528 + Linear 325), matching the main text, Fig 2, Table A.1, and the released code; the Checklist's "~1.1K" was a stale rounding and we will correct it. The reviewer's prompt on the SR-MoA figure was helpful: rechecking Table F.2, the referent is over RR-MoA (SR-MoA beats RR-MoA on all six datasets), and the range itself is imprecise, so we will correct "13-42%" to the exact 23-38% and keep the over-RR-MoA referent explicit. We will also remove the stray parenthesis in R(D) and standardize "fine-tuning."

**Q1 (input length 512 / horizon 96).** Horizon is already varied over H∈{96,192,336,720} (RR-MoA 12/12 vs best fixed; Residual-IA+ 6/6 at H=192). [NEW] We add an input-length ablation (L∈{96,192,336,512}, 6 datasets, 3 seeds): routing never collapses (entropy 0.98-1.48 at every L), raw routing beats the normalized-routing control at all 24 cells, and beats the best fixed adapter at 70/72. Conclusions hold on both axes.

**Q2 (α inconsistency).** Thank you, this is a wording slip. α is initialized at σ(0)=0.5 (the logit is a parameter at 0.0); 0.492 is the mean α at the end of the first logged epoch, after one epoch has moved it below 0.5, not the initialization (trajectory 0.5 → 0.492 → 0.468). We will correct the wording.

**On significance.** The durable contribution is the diagnosis and its predictor, and the reframing above sharpens rather than shrinks it. Normalization-induced routing collapse is a real, mechanistically-explained failure of the standard MoE-adapter upgrade on the dominant instance-normalized TSFM class. R(D) turns that diagnosis into an actionable, training-free tool: computed from raw statistics before any training, it predicts whether raw routing will help on a new dataset (ρ=-0.88 across nine datasets), and equally where it will not (the Traffic null, R=0.14, predicted a priori and confirmed). This go/no-go test transfers beyond our six benchmarks and beyond our specific router, since two architecturally distinct variants (SR-MoA and Residual-IA+) confirm the principle, and it holds regardless of which backbone is best on a given dataset. That, with the raw-routing intervention, is the contribution we ask the reader to take from the paper.

Given the corrected DLinear framing (Residual-IA+ outperforms DLinear 65:11, already in App. P), the re-scoped R(D) account, the added input-length ablation, and the fixes to every minor point raised, and given the reviewer's kind indication that addressing the concerns would raise the score, we would be grateful for a reconsideration of the rating.

**Response to Reviewer 8b2Z**

We thank the reviewer for the constructive assessment and for highlighting the practical value of the signal-ratio metric. Two framing notes upfront. First, many of the concerns are answered by experiments already in the submission (memory, expert scaling, other normalizers, applying raw routing to an existing MoE, a vision replication); where they were hard to find, that is a presentation gap, not missing substance, and we will fix it in the camera-ready. Second, where a concern asked for something genuinely new (an interventional LayerNorm swap, 200-epoch convergence, a significance re-analysis), we ran it, tagged [NEW] below. We address each point.

**W1 (memory of raw routing).** The phrase "routing on raw inputs" sounds memory-heavy, but the design is the opposite: the router reads a single univariate length-L window and is an 853-parameter Conv1d gate (0.002% of the ~40M backbone, 57× smaller than a 49K DLinear), adding <0.1 ms to the backbone's 52.9 ms forward pass. Total overhead across all three variants is +5.9% latency and +6 MB on a 359 MB backbone (Table B.1); peak memory is set by the frozen backbone every adapter method already loads.

**W2 (dataset-distributional / feature-asymmetry factors).** A fair ask. R(D) is in fact a dataset-distributional quantity, computed from raw statistics and predicting per-dataset vulnerability (ρ=-0.88, n=9), with Traffic (R=0.14) and Solar (R=0.06) the boundary/outlier cases; Appendix D.1 adds rate-distortion and information-bottleneck framings toward a broader account. We agree feature asymmetries beyond location-scale are not yet formalized, and our own ablations already show the operative routing signal is broader than (μ,σ) (App. F, SSR +48%); formalizing that is valuable future theory.

**W3 (scaling experts → router-input dimensionality / bandwidth).** In a standard MoE the router input grows with the expert count; here it does not. The router input is the raw window and is independent of K; only the K-way logit layer (64→K) grows, which is negligible. Because routing is Top-2, exactly two experts execute per sample regardless of K, so both active compute and memory traffic are O(2), not O(K). Table I.2 (K∈{1..10}) is the empirical stability check (within ±10% for K≥2). Expert count therefore creates no router-input or bandwidth bottleneck by construction; larger learned or dynamically-generated pools beyond K=10 are future work.

**W4 (other normalizers: BatchNorm / LayerNorm / RMSNorm).** App. H tests this interventionally: swapping RevIN for BatchNorm1d (entropy 0.62→0.004) and GroupNorm (0.51→0.000) yields identical collapse, while removing normalization keeps it healthy (0.82). [NEW] To match this rigor for LayerNorm, we also swap a LayerNorm into MOMENT's input-normalization position (same App. H protocol): it collapses identically (entropy → 0.000), with the no-normalization control healthy at 0.825. The apparent tension with our LayerNorm/RMSNorm negative controls (Chronos, Timer-XL) is resolved by where the norm sits: at the input position it strips per-window statistics and collapses; encoder-internal LayerNorm/RMSNorm do not strip the router's input and do not collapse. The rule is whether the normalizer strips routing-relevant statistics at the router's input.

**W5 (only forecasting / imputation).** Beyond forecasting on six datasets and imputation (Table J, 7/8 wins), [NEW] a classification mechanism-check on three UEA datasets shows routing entropy stays healthy (1.46-1.59, no collapse), so the anti-collapse mechanism is not forecasting-specific; we scope this to mechanism-generalization since frozen features cap absolute accuracy. [NEW] An input-length ablation (L∈{96,192,336,512}, 72 runs) shows no collapse at any L and raw > normalized routing at all 24 cells. Anomaly detection remains honest future work.

**W6 / Q3 (few epochs / convergence).** The complex dual-stream Residual-IA+ reaches its validation optimum early and overfits by 50 epochs; the simpler RR-MoA is robust to long training. Extending full fine-tuning to 50 and 100 epochs (90-config sweep) still loses to 15-epoch frozen RR-MoA by 33-71% (App. O). [NEW] We train RR-MoA to 200 epochs on ETTh1, ETTm1, Weather and Electricity (the dataset flagged as slowest to converge; 3 seeds each): routing never collapses (seed-mean entropy 1.02-1.34, minimum 0.87 across all 12 runs), and MSE is stable-to-improved versus 15 epochs (ETTh1 0.680→0.646, ETTm1 0.564→0.493). The reported 15-epoch numbers are conservative, not a convergence artifact.

**W7 (statistical corrections may be too conservative).** You are right that an over-conservative correction risks false negatives; we address both directions. [NEW] (i) Our claimed effect is correction-immaterial: the pooled Wilcoxon signed-rank on the RR-MoA-vs-best-fixed cells gives p ≈ 3×10^-11 uncorrected, so Bonferroni over every comparison in the paper still leaves it below 10^-9, and Holm/BH only lower it further. A per-dataset Wilcoxon with 3-7 seeds is limited by seed count, not effect size (an n=3 signed-rank floors at p=0.125), which is why the headline significance is the pooled test plus the 54/54 win-count rather than per-dataset p-values. (ii) The boundary null is genuine: on Traffic (R=0.14) RR-MoA does not beat the best fixed adapter even under the most powerful uncorrected test (+2.9%, p=0.88). We will report uncorrected and Holm/BH values alongside Bonferroni.

**Q1 (apply raw routing to an existing MoE, e.g. AdaMix).** We do exactly this. AdaMix-Raw swaps only AdaMix's hidden-state router for a raw-input router, leaving its experts and training loop unchanged: routing entropy recovers from near-collapse to near-uniform (0.49→1.55) and MSE improves 42-88% across all 12 cells. This isolates the router input as the dominant cause, exactly the clarification requested.

**Q2 (generality to image / other domains).** App. H.1 replicates the mechanism in vision: a ViT-B/16 with InstanceNorm1d on patch embeddings collapses (0.000), while ResNet-18 does not (its InstanceNorm2d strips statistics that do not carry the routing signal), matching the theory across modality.

**On significance.** We are glad the review already recognizes the signal-ratio's value ("predicting dataset vulnerability prior to training... practical value beyond the specific method"). We would stress that this is the paper's most transferable contribution: R(D) is training-free and computed a priori (ρ=-0.88, n=9), so a practitioner can decide before any training whether raw routing will help on a new dataset, and it correctly abstains where it will not (the Traffic null, R=0.14). Together with the collapse diagnosis it explains, that is a reusable result for the TSFM-adapter community, independent of which backbone is best on a given dataset. And the diagnosis is general, not LTSF-specific: it reproduces under BatchNorm and GroupNorm and in a vision modality (App. H, H.1), so the significance extends to any instance-normalized backbone paired with a mixture head.

Given that the memory, expert-scaling, normalizer-generality, task-diversity, convergence, and statistical concerns are now addressed, several of them from evidence already in the submission, we would be grateful if the reviewer would consider re-evaluating the score.

**Response to Reviewer Pm4m**

We thank the reviewer for the detailed, fair reading, and for noting that concerns, once addressed, would raise the score. We answer every point. All supporting results are already in the submitted paper unless tagged [NEW]; because the PDF is frozen, presentation fixes are stated as camera-ready commitments ("we will...").

**W1 (framing / DLinear).** This is the central point and we treat it as such, but one correction changes the conclusion. We appreciate the reviewer holding the method to a from-scratch DLinear, and the observation is exactly right for RR-MoA-proper, the minimal diagnostic probe whose only role is to isolate the router input. We would gently add that it does not carry over to the method we deploy: Residual-IA+, reported in the submitted Appendix P, matches or beats DLinear rather than trailing it:
- 65 significant wins vs 11 losses (5.9:1); 107/123 match-or-beat (87%) across 6 backbones × 6 datasets × 4 horizons.
- 6/6 at the H=192 deployment horizon; MOMENT-large 23/24 with zero losses (16 significant wins); Moirai-MoE 15/15 (100%).
- It dominates on non-stationary data at long horizons (ETTm2 -27.0% at H=720; ETTh2 wins at all four horizons).
- Even at the single least-favorable slice cited (MOMENT-small, H=96), the net mean gap is -2.8%, a win, with ETTh1 the only loss.

We read the criticism as fair about our framing, not our evidence: we led with "5/6 match-or-beat" and titled the appendix "Closing the DLinear Gap," which foregrounded the one losing cell (ETTh1/H=96). We will (i) promote the full grid and the 65:11 win-count into the main text, (ii) retitle to the outperformance the numbers show, and (iii) reframe the abstract's DLinear comparison as scope, not deficit: "Because the router isolates the collapse mechanism rather than maximizing accuracy, the minimal RR-MoA probe trails a from-scratch DLinear on linear-dominated datasets; our deployment adapter Residual-IA+ removes this gap, matching or beating DLinear across six backbones and four horizons." We also accept the narrow, true version: RR-MoA-proper does trail DLinear in absolute MSE, sharpest on ETTh1/H=96, and we will introduce it plainly as a diagnostic instrument, not an accuracy claim.

**W2 (Figure 2).** Agreed. We will redraw Figure 2 at larger size with non-overlapping modules and a clearer depiction of the raw-router and frozen-expert paths.

**W3 (Moirai gains without collapse).** A fair distinction. Moirai applies non-learnable instance normalization (Kim et al. 2022, i.e. RevIN) to inputs/outputs, stripping the same per-window location-scale we study, minus the learnable affine. Raw routing recovers the stripped signal there by the same input-side mechanism, while the absence of learnable affine is exactly why AdaMix does not collapse on Moirai: the sudden collapse is driven by gradient co-adaptation and requires a learnable affine. The unified claim is "raw routing helps whenever per-window statistics are stripped from the router's input," and collapse is the severe failure mode that additionally requires learnable affine. We will present the cross-backbone results as consistent with the diagnosis rather than as uniform collapse-repair, and add the Moirai citation.

**W4 (heavy tuning; generalization beyond six).** On "heavy tuning": the 546-run sweep was development effort, and we agree it should not be presented as a SOTA search. We would add that the endpoint is not merely parity with DLinear but a win (65:11), and that the recipe is fixed rather than per-dataset tuned. [NEW] Applied unchanged (gate-init b=-2, 5-epoch warmup, shared NLinear, validation early-stop) to three datasets it had never seen, Residual-IA+ matches or beats DLinear on 8/9 (dataset, seed) cells: Solar 3/3 (-9.5%), Traffic 3/3 (parity), Exchange 2/3, no collapse. A recipe that transfers to unseen data without re-tuning speaks against the dataset-specific-engineering reading, and directly addresses "generalization beyond these six is unclear."

On "the raw branch does the work; the TSFM is dead weight (P.3)": one clarification we should have made explicit. P.3's "dead weight" verdict is measured against the intermediate Dual-Stream (ETTh2 0.452, ETTm2 0.252), not the final Residual-IA+ (ETTh2 0.346, ETTm2 0.188), and that intermediate architecture itself loses to DLinear. P.3's own backbone-free Raw-MLP MoE loses to DLinear by +11.2% on all six datasets: remove the TSFM and you fall behind DLinear; it is the TSFM-inclusive Residual-IA+ that gets ahead. [NEW] We ran the clean isolation directly, Residual-IA+ vs an identical-budget backbone-free Raw-MLP MoE, holding the raw branch fixed and toggling only the backbone, at H=192 (where the paper reports the backbone contributes maximally): Residual-IA+ wins 18/18 (mean -11.8%), including ETTh2/ETTm2/Electricity, the very datasets flagged as dead-weight at H=96, while still matching or beating a 49K DLinear. The backbone's contribution is therefore horizon-dependent: small at H=96 on linear-dominated data, decisively positive at H≥192.

**W5 ((μ,σ) tension).** The tension is real, and re-scoping Observation 1 resolves it: R(D) is the ratio of routing-discriminative variance in the instance-norm-removable component (location-scale) to that in the surviving component (shape), not a claim that (μ,σ) is the whole routing signal. When the ratio is high, stripping (μ,σ) removes most of the routing signal and routing collapses; when it is low (Traffic, R=0.14) the signal lives in the surviving shape, so stripping does not hurt and RR-MoA correctly does not improve. This is exactly consistent with the ablations cited: [μ,σ]-only routing degrades +48% (SSR) and temporal shuffling moves performance ≤3%. We will re-scope Observation 1 explicitly as a vulnerability predictor / lower bound, not a sufficiency claim.

**W6 (minor).** All accepted. The router parameter count is 853 (Conv1d 528 + Linear 325), matching the main text, Fig 2, Table A.1, and the released code; the Checklist's "~1.1K" was a stale rounding and we will correct it. The reviewer's prompt on the SR-MoA figure was helpful: rechecking Table F.2, the referent is over RR-MoA (SR-MoA beats RR-MoA on all six datasets), and the range itself is imprecise, so we will correct "13-42%" to the exact 23-38% and keep the over-RR-MoA referent explicit. We will also remove the stray parenthesis in R(D) and standardize "fine-tuning."

**Q1 (input length 512 / horizon 96).** The input length is indeed fixed at 512, and the reviewer is right to probe it. Multi-horizon results, though, are already in the submitted paper (Table 14: RR-MoA 12/12 vs best fixed; Residual-IA+ 6/6 at H=192, over H∈{96,192,336,720}); we may not have surfaced them prominently enough. [NEW] For input length we add an ablation (L∈{96,192,336,512}, 6 datasets, 3 seeds): routing never collapses (entropy 0.98-1.48 at every L), raw routing beats the normalized-routing control at all 24 cells, and beats the best fixed adapter at 70/72. Conclusions hold on both axes.

**Q2 (α inconsistency).** Thank you, this is a wording slip. α is initialized at σ(0)=0.5 (the logit is a parameter at 0.0); 0.492 is the mean α at the end of the first logged epoch, after one epoch has moved it below 0.5, not the initialization (trajectory 0.5 → 0.492 → 0.468). We will correct the wording.

**On significance.** The durable contribution is the diagnosis and its predictor, and the reframing above sharpens rather than shrinks it. Normalization-induced routing collapse is a real, mechanistically-explained failure of the standard MoE-adapter upgrade on the dominant instance-normalized TSFM class. R(D) turns that diagnosis into an actionable, training-free tool: computed from raw statistics before any training, it predicts whether raw routing will help on a new dataset (ρ=-0.88 across nine datasets), and equally where it will not (the Traffic null, R=0.14, predicted a priori and confirmed). **Response to Reviewer 8b2Z**

We thank the reviewer for the constructive assessment and for highlighting the practical value of the signal-ratio metric. Two framing notes upfront. First, many of the concerns are answered by experiments already in the submission (memory, expert scaling, other normalizers, applying raw routing to an existing MoE, a vision replication); where they were hard to find, that is a presentation gap, not missing substance, and we will fix it in the camera-ready. Second, where a concern asked for something genuinely new (an interventional LayerNorm swap, 200-epoch convergence, a significance re-analysis), we ran it, tagged [NEW] below. We address each point.

**W1 (memory of raw routing).** We can see why "routing on raw inputs" sounds memory-heavy; in practice the footprint is small. The router reads a single univariate length-L window and is an 853-parameter Conv1d gate (0.002% of the ~40M backbone, 57× smaller than a 49K DLinear), adding <0.1 ms to the backbone's 52.9 ms forward pass. Total overhead across all three variants is +5.9% latency and +6 MB on a 359 MB backbone (Table B.1); peak memory is set by the frozen backbone every adapter method already loads.

**W2 (dataset-distributional / feature-asymmetry factors).** A fair ask. R(D) is in fact a dataset-distributional quantity, computed from raw statistics and predicting per-dataset vulnerability (ρ=-0.88, n=9), with Traffic (R=0.14) and Solar (R=0.06) the boundary/outlier cases; Appendix D.1 adds rate-distortion and information-bottleneck framings toward a broader account. We agree feature asymmetries beyond location-scale are not yet formalized, and our own ablations already show the operative routing signal is broader than (μ,σ) (App. F, SSR +48%); formalizing that is valuable future theory.

**W3 (scaling experts → router-input dimensionality / bandwidth).** This is a natural worry, since in a standard MoE the router input does grow with the expert count. In our design it does not: The router input is the raw window and is independent of K; only the K-way logit layer (64→K) grows, which is negligible. Because routing is Top-2, exactly two experts execute per sample regardless of K, so both active compute and memory traffic are O(2), not O(K). Table I.2 (K∈{1..10}) is the empirical stability check (within ±10% for K≥2). Expert count therefore creates no router-input or bandwidth bottleneck by construction; larger learned or dynamically-generated pools beyond K=10 are future work.

**W4 (other normalizers: BatchNorm / LayerNorm / RMSNorm).** This is a natural question, and the submitted App. H already tests it interventionally: swapping RevIN for BatchNorm1d (entropy 0.62→0.004) and GroupNorm (0.51→0.000) yields identical collapse, while removing normalization keeps it healthy (0.82). [NEW] To match this rigor for LayerNorm, we also swap a LayerNorm into MOMENT's input-normalization position (same App. H protocol): it collapses identically (entropy → 0.000), with the no-normalization control healthy at 0.825. The apparent tension with our LayerNorm/RMSNorm negative controls (Chronos, Timer-XL) is resolved by where the norm sits: at the input position it strips per-window statistics and collapses; encoder-internal LayerNorm/RMSNorm do not strip the router's input and do not collapse. The rule is whether the normalizer strips routing-relevant statistics at the router's input.

**W5 (only forecasting / imputation).** Beyond forecasting on six datasets and imputation (Table J, 7/8 wins), [NEW] a classification mechanism-check on three UEA datasets shows routing entropy stays healthy (1.46-1.59, no collapse), so the anti-collapse mechanism is not forecasting-specific; we scope this to mechanism-generalization since frozen features cap absolute accuracy. [NEW] An input-length ablation (L∈{96,192,336,512}, 72 runs) shows no collapse at any L and raw > normalized routing at all 24 cells. Anomaly detection remains honest future work.

**W6 / Q3 (few epochs / convergence).** The complex dual-stream Residual-IA+ reaches its validation optimum early and overfits by 50 epochs; the simpler RR-MoA is robust to long training. Extending full fine-tuning to 50 and 100 epochs (90-config sweep) still loses to 15-epoch frozen RR-MoA by 33-71% (App. O). [NEW] We train RR-MoA to 200 epochs on ETTh1, ETTm1, Weather and Electricity (the dataset flagged as slowest to converge; 3 seeds each): routing never collapses (seed-mean entropy 1.02-1.34, minimum 0.87 across all 12 runs), and MSE is stable-to-improved versus 15 epochs (ETTh1 0.680→0.646, ETTm1 0.564→0.493). The reported 15-epoch numbers are conservative, not a convergence artifact.

**W7 (statistical corrections may be too conservative).** You are right that an over-conservative correction risks false negatives; we address both directions. [NEW] (i) Our claimed effect is correction-immaterial: the pooled Wilcoxon signed-rank on the RR-MoA-vs-best-fixed cells gives p ≈ 3×10^-11 uncorrected, so Bonferroni over every comparison in the paper still leaves it below 10^-9, and Holm/BH only lower it further. A per-dataset Wilcoxon with 3-7 seeds is limited by seed count, not effect size (an n=3 signed-rank floors at p=0.125), which is why the headline significance is the pooled test plus the 54/54 win-count rather than per-dataset p-values. (ii) The boundary null is genuine: on Traffic (R=0.14) RR-MoA does not beat the best fixed adapter even under the most powerful uncorrected test (+2.9%, p=0.88). We will report uncorrected and Holm/BH values alongside Bonferroni.

This isolates the router input as the dominant cause, exactly the clarification requested.

All four artifacts are now clean and compliant. Here's what I verified and fixed against the actual OpenReview rules.

**The rule (from the FAQ chain):** OpenReview renders **CommonMark 0.29 + MathJax**, with **inline HTML and images disabled**, and the LaTeX doc warns that Markdown can mangle backslash-TeX.

**What was already fine:** no underscores, dollar signs, or pipes anywhere; single newlines correctly collapse to spaces (flowing paragraphs); the `**bold**` section labels and inline `(i)/(ii)` markers don't trigger stray headers or lists.

**What I fixed:**
- **Power-of-ten values** (`3×10^-11`, `10^-9`) rendered as literal carets → converted to **Unicode superscripts** (`3×10⁻¹¹`, `10⁻⁹`). I chose Unicode over `$…$` LaTeX deliberately: it renders as true superscript with zero MathJax/backslash-escaping risk, which the OpenReview LaTeX doc specifically warns about. LaTeX is *permitted*, not required — correct rendering is the goal.
- **Stray angle brackets** (`<0.1 ms`, `raw > normalized`) → "under 0.1 ms", "raw beats normalized". Harmless with HTML off, but cleaner and unambiguous.
- **Pm4m bullet list** → added a defensive blank line before it so it renders as a list under any parser.
- Applied the same sweep to the **discussion kit** (its primary reply/fact-sheet get pasted too).

**Final state — all zero hazards, all under 10k:**
| File | Chars | Hazards |
|---|---|---|
| response_pm4m.md | 8,678 | none |
| response_jemj.md | 2,508 | none |
| response_8b2z.md | 7,509 | none |
| discussion_8b2z.md | (kit) | none |

Retained Unicode (ρ, μ, σ, ×, ≈, ≤, →, ∈) is valid CommonMark text and renders as-is — no need to LaTeX-ify it.

These edits are uncommitted. Want me to `/commit-push`?

**Response to Reviewer Pm4m**

We thank the reviewer for the detailed, fair reading, and for noting that concerns, once addressed, would raise the score. We answer every point. All supporting results are already in the submitted paper unless tagged [NEW]; because the PDF is frozen, presentation fixes are stated as camera-ready commitments ("we will...").

**W1 (framing / DLinear).** This is the central point and we treat it as such, but one correction changes the conclusion. We appreciate the reviewer holding the method to a from-scratch DLinear, and the observation is exactly right for RR-MoA-proper, the minimal diagnostic probe whose only role is to isolate the router input. We would gently add that it does not carry over to the method we deploy: Residual-IA+, reported in the submitted Appendix P, matches or beats DLinear rather than trailing it:

- 65 significant wins vs 11 losses (5.9:1); 107/123 match-or-beat (87%) across 6 backbones × 6 datasets × 4 horizons.
- 6/6 at the H=192 deployment horizon; MOMENT-large 23/24 with zero losses (16 significant wins); Moirai-MoE 15/15 (100%).
- It dominates on non-stationary data at long horizons (ETTm2 -27.0% at H=720; ETTh2 wins at all four horizons).
- Even at the single least-favorable slice cited (MOMENT-small, H=96), the net mean gap is -2.8%, a win, with ETTh1 the only loss.

We read the criticism as fair about our framing, not our evidence: we led with "5/6 match-or-beat" and titled the appendix "Closing the DLinear Gap," which foregrounded the one losing cell (ETTh1/H=96). We will (i) promote the full grid and the 65:11 win-count into the main text, (ii) retitle to the outperformance the numbers show, and (iii) reframe the abstract's DLinear comparison as scope, not deficit: "Because the router isolates the collapse mechanism rather than maximizing accuracy, the minimal RR-MoA probe trails a from-scratch DLinear on linear-dominated datasets; our deployment adapter Residual-IA+ removes this gap, matching or beating DLinear across six backbones and four horizons." We also accept the narrow, true version: RR-MoA-proper does trail DLinear in absolute MSE, sharpest on ETTh1/H=96, and we will introduce it plainly as a diagnostic instrument, not an accuracy claim.

**W2 (Figure 2).** Agreed. We will redraw Figure 2 at larger size with non-overlapping modules and a clearer depiction of the raw-router and frozen-expert paths.

**W3 (Moirai gains without collapse).** A fair distinction. Moirai applies non-learnable instance normalization (Kim et al. 2022, i.e. RevIN) to inputs/outputs, stripping the same per-window location-scale we study, minus the learnable affine. Raw routing recovers the stripped signal there by the same input-side mechanism, while the absence of learnable affine is exactly why AdaMix does not collapse on Moirai: the sudden collapse is driven by gradient co-adaptation and requires a learnable affine. The unified claim is "raw routing helps whenever per-window statistics are stripped from the router's input," and collapse is the severe failure mode that additionally requires learnable affine. We will present the cross-backbone results as consistent with the diagnosis rather than as uniform collapse-repair, and add the Moirai citation.

**W4 (heavy tuning; generalization beyond six).** On "heavy tuning": the 546-run sweep was development effort, and we agree it should not be presented as a SOTA search. We would add that the endpoint is not merely parity with DLinear but a win (65:11), and that the recipe is fixed rather than per-dataset tuned. [NEW] Applied unchanged (gate-init b=-2, 5-epoch warmup, shared NLinear, validation early-stop) to three datasets it had never seen, Residual-IA+ matches or beats DLinear on 8/9 (dataset, seed) cells: Solar 3/3 (-9.5%), Traffic 3/3 (parity), Exchange 2/3, no collapse. A recipe that transfers to unseen data without re-tuning speaks against the dataset-specific-engineering reading, and directly addresses "generalization beyond these six is unclear."

On "the raw branch does the work; the TSFM is dead weight (P.3)": one clarification we should have made explicit. P.3's "dead weight" verdict is measured against the intermediate Dual-Stream (ETTh2 0.452, ETTm2 0.252), not the final Residual-IA+ (ETTh2 0.346, ETTm2 0.188), and that intermediate architecture itself loses to DLinear. P.3's own backbone-free Raw-MLP MoE loses to DLinear by +11.2% on all six datasets: remove the TSFM and you fall behind DLinear; it is the TSFM-inclusive Residual-IA+ that gets ahead. [NEW] We ran the clean isolation directly, Residual-IA+ vs an identical-budget backbone-free Raw-MLP MoE, holding the raw branch fixed and toggling only the backbone, at H=192 (where the paper reports the backbone contributes maximally): Residual-IA+ wins 18/18 (mean -11.8%), including ETTh2/ETTm2/Electricity, the very datasets flagged as dead-weight at H=96, while still matching or beating a 49K DLinear. The backbone's contribution is therefore horizon-dependent: small at H=96 on linear-dominated data, decisively positive at H≥192.

**W5 ((μ,σ) tension).** The tension is real, and re-scoping Observation 1 resolves it: R(D) is the ratio of routing-discriminative variance in the instance-norm-removable component (location-scale) to that in the surviving component (shape), not a claim that (μ,σ) is the whole routing signal. When the ratio is high, stripping (μ,σ) removes most of the routing signal and routing collapses; when it is low (Traffic, R=0.14) the signal lives in the surviving shape, so stripping does not hurt and RR-MoA correctly does not improve. This is exactly consistent with the ablations cited: [μ,σ]-only routing degrades +48% (SSR) and temporal shuffling moves performance ≤3%. We will re-scope Observation 1 explicitly as a vulnerability predictor / lower bound, not a sufficiency claim.

**W6 (minor).** All accepted. The router parameter count is 853 (Conv1d 528 + Linear 325), matching the main text, Fig 2, Table A.1, and the released code; the Checklist's "~1.1K" was a stale rounding and we will correct it. The reviewer's prompt on the SR-MoA figure was helpful: rechecking Table F.2, the referent is over RR-MoA (SR-MoA beats RR-MoA on all six datasets), and the range itself is imprecise, so we will correct "13-42%" to the exact 23-38% and keep the over-RR-MoA referent explicit. We will also remove the stray parenthesis in R(D) and standardize "fine-tuning."

**Q1 (input length 512 / horizon 96).** The input length is indeed fixed at 512, and the reviewer is right to probe it. Multi-horizon results, though, are already in the submitted paper (Table 14: RR-MoA 12/12 vs best fixed; Residual-IA+ 6/6 at H=192, over H∈{96,192,336,720}); we may not have surfaced them prominently enough. [NEW] For input length we add an ablation (L∈{96,192,336,512}, 6 datasets, 3 seeds): routing never collapses (entropy 0.98-1.48 at every L), raw routing beats the normalized-routing control at all 24 cells, and beats the best fixed adapter at 70/72. Conclusions hold on both axes.

**Q2 (α inconsistency).** Thank you, this is a wording slip. α is initialized at σ(0)=0.5 (the logit is a parameter at 0.0); 0.492 is the mean α at the end of the first logged epoch, after one epoch has moved it below 0.5, not the initialization (trajectory 0.5 → 0.492 → 0.468). We will correct the wording.

**On significance.** The durable contribution is the diagnosis and its predictor, and the reframing above sharpens rather than shrinks it. Normalization-induced routing collapse is a real, mechanistically-explained failure of the standard MoE-adapter upgrade on the dominant instance-normalized TSFM class. R(D) turns that diagnosis into an actionable, training-free tool: computed from raw statistics before any training, it predicts whether raw routing will help on a new dataset (ρ=-0.88 across nine datasets), and equally where it will not (the Traffic null, R=0.14, predicted a priori and confirmed). This go/no-go test transfers beyond our six benchmarks and beyond our specific router, since two architecturally distinct variants (SR-MoA and Residual-IA+) confirm the principle, and it holds regardless of which backbone is best on a given dataset. That, with the raw-routing intervention, is the contribution we ask the reader to take from the paper.

Given the corrected DLinear framing (Residual-IA+ outperforms DLinear 65:11, already in App. P), the re-scoped R(D) account, the added input-length ablation, and the fixes to every minor point raised, and given the reviewer's kind indication that addressing the concerns would raise the score, we would be grateful for a reconsideration of the rating.

**Response to Reviewer Pm4m**

We thank the reviewer for the detailed, fair reading, and for noting that concerns, once addressed, would raise the score. We address every point below; all supporting results are already in the submitted paper unless tagged [NEW].

**W1 (framing / DLinear).** This is the central point and we treat it as such, but one correction changes the conclusion. We appreciate the reviewer holding the method to a from-scratch DLinear, and the observation is exactly right for RR-MoA-proper, the minimal diagnostic probe whose only role is to isolate the router input. We would gently add that it does not carry over to the method we deploy: Residual-IA+, reported in the submitted Appendix P, matches or beats DLinear rather than trailing it:

- 65 significant wins vs 11 losses (5.9:1); 107/123 match-or-beat (87%) across 6 backbones × 6 datasets × 4 horizons.
- 6/6 at the H=192 deployment horizon; MOMENT-large 23/24 with zero losses (16 significant wins); Moirai-MoE 15/15 (100%).
- It dominates on non-stationary data at long horizons (ETTm2 -27.0% at H=720; ETTh2 wins at all four horizons).
- Even at the single least-favorable slice cited (MOMENT-small, H=96), the net mean gap is -2.8%, a win, with ETTh1 the only loss.

We read the criticism as fair about our framing, not our evidence: we led with "5/6 match-or-beat" and titled the appendix "Closing the DLinear Gap," which foregrounded the one losing cell (ETTh1/H=96). We will (i) promote the full grid and the 65:11 win-count into the main text, (ii) retitle to the outperformance the numbers show, and (iii) reframe the abstract's DLinear comparison as scope, not deficit: "Because the router isolates the collapse mechanism rather than maximizing accuracy, the minimal RR-MoA probe trails a from-scratch DLinear on linear-dominated datasets; our deployment adapter Residual-IA+ removes this gap, matching or beating DLinear across six backbones and four horizons." We also accept the narrow, true version: RR-MoA-proper does trail DLinear in absolute MSE, sharpest on ETTh1/H=96, and we will introduce it plainly as a diagnostic instrument, not an accuracy claim.

**W2 (Figure 2).** Agreed. We will redraw Figure 2 at larger size with non-overlapping modules and a clearer depiction of the raw-router and frozen-expert paths.

**W3 (Moirai gains without collapse).** A fair distinction. Moirai applies non-learnable instance normalization (Kim et al. 2022, i.e. RevIN) to inputs/outputs, stripping the same per-window location-scale we study, minus the learnable affine. Raw routing recovers the stripped signal there by the same input-side mechanism, while the absence of learnable affine is exactly why AdaMix does not collapse on Moirai: the sudden collapse is driven by gradient co-adaptation and requires a learnable affine. The unified claim is "raw routing helps whenever per-window statistics are stripped from the router's input," and collapse is the severe failure mode that additionally requires learnable affine. We will present the cross-backbone results as consistent with the diagnosis rather than as uniform collapse-repair, and add the Moirai citation.

**W4 (heavy tuning; generalization beyond six).** On "heavy tuning": the 546-run sweep was development effort, and we agree it should not be presented as a SOTA search. We would add that the endpoint is not merely parity with DLinear but a win (65:11), and that the recipe is fixed rather than per-dataset tuned. [NEW] Applied unchanged (gate-init b=-2, 5-epoch warmup, shared NLinear, validation early-stop) to three datasets it had never seen, Residual-IA+ matches or beats DLinear on 8/9 (dataset, seed) cells: Solar 3/3 (-9.5%), Traffic 3/3 (parity), Exchange 2/3, no collapse. A recipe that transfers to unseen data without re-tuning speaks against the dataset-specific-engineering reading, and directly addresses "generalization beyond these six is unclear."

On "the raw branch does the work; the TSFM is dead weight (P.3)": one clarification we should have made explicit. P.3's "dead weight" verdict is measured against the intermediate Dual-Stream (ETTh2 0.452, ETTm2 0.252), not the final Residual-IA+ (ETTh2 0.346, ETTm2 0.188), and that intermediate architecture itself loses to DLinear. P.3's own backbone-free Raw-MLP MoE loses to DLinear by +11.2% on all six datasets: remove the TSFM and you fall behind DLinear; it is the TSFM-inclusive Residual-IA+ that gets ahead. [NEW] We ran the clean isolation directly, Residual-IA+ vs an identical-budget backbone-free Raw-MLP MoE, holding the raw branch fixed and toggling only the backbone, at H=192 (where the paper reports the backbone contributes maximally): Residual-IA+ wins 18/18 (mean -11.8%), including ETTh2/ETTm2/Electricity, the very datasets flagged as dead-weight at H=96, while still matching or beating a 49K DLinear. The backbone's contribution is therefore horizon-dependent: small at H=96 on linear-dominated data, decisively positive at H≥192.

**W5 ((μ,σ) tension).** The tension is real, and re-scoping Observation 1 resolves it: R(D) is the ratio of routing-discriminative variance in the instance-norm-removable component (location-scale) to that in the surviving component (shape), not a claim that (μ,σ) is the whole routing signal. When the ratio is high, stripping (μ,σ) removes most of the routing signal and routing collapses; when it is low (Traffic, R=0.14) the signal lives in the surviving shape, so stripping does not hurt and RR-MoA correctly does not improve. This is exactly consistent with the ablations cited: [μ,σ]-only routing degrades +48% (SSR) and temporal shuffling moves performance ≤3%. We will re-scope Observation 1 explicitly as a vulnerability predictor / lower bound, not a sufficiency claim.

**W6 (minor).** All accepted. The router parameter count is 853 (Conv1d 528 + Linear 325), matching the main text, Fig 2, Table A.1, and the released code; the Checklist's "~1.1K" was a stale rounding and we will correct it. The reviewer's prompt on the SR-MoA figure was helpful: rechecking Table F.2, the referent is over RR-MoA (SR-MoA beats RR-MoA on all six datasets), and the range itself is imprecise, so we will correct "13-42%" to the exact 23-38% and keep the over-RR-MoA referent explicit. We will also remove the stray parenthesis in R(D) and standardize "fine-tuning."

**Q1 (input length 512 / horizon 96).** The input length is indeed fixed at 512, and the reviewer is right to probe it. Multi-horizon results, though, are already in the submitted paper (Table 14: RR-MoA 12/12 vs best fixed; Residual-IA+ 6/6 at H=192, over H∈{96,192,336,720}); we may not have surfaced them prominently enough. [NEW] For input length we add an ablation (L∈{96,192,336,512}, 6 datasets, 3 seeds): routing never collapses (entropy 0.98-1.48 at every L), raw routing beats the normalized-routing control at all 24 cells, and beats the best fixed adapter at 70/72. Conclusions hold on both axes.

**Q2 (α inconsistency).** Thank you, this is a wording slip. α is initialized at σ(0)=0.5 (the logit is a parameter at 0.0); 0.492 is the mean α at the end of the first logged epoch, after one epoch has moved it below 0.5, not the initialization (trajectory 0.5 → 0.492 → 0.468). We will correct the wording.

**On significance.** The durable contribution is the diagnosis and its predictor, and the reframing above sharpens rather than shrinks it. Normalization-induced routing collapse is a real, mechanistically-explained failure of the standard MoE-adapter upgrade on the dominant instance-normalized TSFM class. R(D) turns that diagnosis into an actionable, training-free tool: computed from raw statistics before any training, it predicts whether raw routing will help on a new dataset (ρ=-0.88 across nine datasets), and equally where it will not (the Traffic null, R=0.14, predicted a priori and confirmed). This go/no-go test transfers beyond our six benchmarks and beyond our specific router, since two architecturally distinct variants (SR-MoA and Residual-IA+) confirm the principle, and it holds regardless of which backbone is best on a given dataset. That, with the raw-routing intervention, is the contribution we ask the reader to take from the paper.

The unified claim is "raw routing helps whenever per-window statistics are stripped from the router's input," and collapse is the severe failure mode that additionally requires learnable affine. We will present the cross-backbone results as consistent with the diagnosis rather than as uniform collapse-repair, and add the Moirai citation.

**W4 (heavy tuning; generalization beyond six).** On "heavy tuning": the 546-run sweep was development effort, and we agree it should not be presented as a SOTA search. We would add that the endpoint is not merely parity with DLinear but a win (65:11), and that the recipe is fixed rather than per-dataset tuned. [NEW] Applied unchanged (gate-init b=-2, 5-epoch warmup, shared NLinear, validation early-stop) to three datasets it had never seen, Residual-IA+ matches or beats DLinear on 8/9 (dataset, seed) cells: Solar 3/3 (-9.5%), Traffic 3/3 (parity), Exchange 2/3, no collapse. A recipe that transfers to unseen data without re-tuning speaks against the dataset-specific-engineering reading, and directly addresses "generalization beyond these six is unclear."

On "the raw branch does the work; the TSFM is dead weight (P.3)": one clarification we should have made explicit. P.3's "dead weight" verdict is measured against the intermediate Dual-Stream (ETTh2 0.452, ETTm2 0.252), not the final Residual-IA+ (ETTh2 0.346, ETTm2 0.188), and that intermediate architecture itself loses to DLinear. P.3's own backbone-free Raw-MLP MoE loses to DLinear by +11.2% on all six datasets: remove the TSFM and you fall behind DLinear; it is the TSFM-inclusive Residual-IA+ that gets ahead. [NEW] We ran the clean isolation directly, Residual-IA+ vs an identical-budget backbone-free Raw-MLP MoE, holding the raw branch fixed and toggling only the backbone, at H=192 (where the paper reports the backbone contributes maximally): Residual-IA+ wins 18/18 (mean -11.8%), including ETTh2/ETTm2/Electricity, the very datasets flagged as dead-weight at H=96, while still matching or beating a 49K DLinear. The backbone's contribution is therefore horizon-dependent: small at H=96 on linear-dominated data, decisively positive at H≥192.

When the ratio is high, stripping (μ,σ) removes most of the routing signal and routing collapses; when it is low (Traffic, R=0.14) the signal lives in the surviving shape, so stripping does not hurt and RR-MoA correctly does not improve. This is exactly consistent with the ablations cited: [μ,σ]-only routing degrades +48% (SSR) and temporal shuffling moves performance ≤3%. We will re-scope Observation 1 explicitly as a vulnerability predictor / lower bound, not a sufficiency claim.

**W6 (minor).** All accepted. The router parameter count is 853 (Conv1d 528 + Linear 325), matching the main text, Fig 2, Table A.1, and the released code; the Checklist's "~1.1K" was a stale rounding and we will correct it. The reviewer's prompt on the SR-MoA figure was helpful: rechecking Table F.2, the referent is over RR-MoA (SR-MoA beats RR-MoA on all six datasets), and the range itself is imprecise, so we will correct "13-42%" to the exact 23-38% and keep the over-RR-MoA referent explicit. We will also remove the stray parenthesis in R(D) and standardize "fine-tuning."

**Q1 (input length 512 / horizon 96).** The input length is indeed fixed at 512, and the reviewer is right to probe it. Multi-horizon results, though, are already in the submitted paper (Table 14: RR-MoA 12/12 vs best fixed; Residual-IA+ 6/6 at H=192, over H∈{96,192,336,720}); we may not have surfaced them prominently enough. [NEW] For input length we add an ablation (L∈{96,192,336,512}, 6 datasets, 3 seeds): routing never collapses (entropy 0.98-1.48 at every L), raw routing beats the normalized-routing control at all 24 cells, and beats the best fixed adapter at 70/72. Conclusions hold on both axes.

We will correct the wording.

**On significance.** The durable contribution is the diagnosis and its predictor, and the reframing above sharpens rather than shrinks it. Normalization-induced routing collapse is a real, mechanistically-explained failure of the standard MoE-adapter upgrade on the dominant instance-normalized TSFM class. R(D) turns that diagnosis into an actionable, training-free tool: computed from raw statistics before any training, it predicts whether raw routing will help on a new dataset (ρ=-0.88 across nine datasets), and equally where it will not (the Traffic null, R=0.14, predicted a priori and confirmed). This go/no-go test transfers beyond our six benchmarks and beyond our specific router, since two architecturally distinct variants (SR-MoA and Residual-IA+) confirm the principle, and it holds regardless of which backbone is best on a given dataset. That, with the raw-routing intervention, is the contribution we ask the reader to take from the paper.

Given the corrected DLinear framing (Residual-IA+ outperforms DLinear 65:11, already in App. P), the re-scoped R(D) account, the added input-length ablation, and the fixes to every minor point raised, and given the reviewer's kind indication that addressing the concerns would raise the score, we would be grateful for a reconsideration of the rating.

**Response to Reviewer Pm4m**

We thank the reviewer for the detailed, fair reading, and for noting that concerns, once addressed, would raise the score. We address every point below; all supporting results are already in the submitted paper unless tagged [NEW].

**W1 (framing / DLinear).** This is the central point and we treat it as such, but one correction changes the conclusion. We appreciate the reviewer holding the method to a from-scratch DLinear, and the observation is exactly right for RR-MoA-proper, the minimal diagnostic probe whose only role is to isolate the router input. We would gently add that it does not carry over to the method we deploy: Residual-IA+, reported in the submitted Appendix P, matches or beats DLinear rather than trailing it:

- 65 significant wins vs 11 losses (5.9:1); 107/123 match-or-beat (87%) across 6 backbones × 6 datasets × 4 horizons.
- 6/6 at the H=192 deployment horizon; MOMENT-large 23/24 with zero losses (16 significant wins); Moirai-MoE 15/15 (100%).
- It dominates on non-stationary data at long horizons (ETTm2 -27.0% at H=720; ETTh2 wins at all four horizons).
- Even at the single least-favorable slice cited (MOMENT-small, H=96), the net mean gap is -2.8%, a win, with ETTh1 the only loss.

**Response to Reviewer Pm4m**

We are grateful for the reviewer's exceptionally close and careful reading: the comments engage the appendix tables and the checklist down to fine details, such as the router parameter count and the α initialization, as attentively as the headline claims, and this is exactly the kind of scrutiny that makes a paper stronger. We also thank the reviewer for noting that addressing these concerns would raise the score. We address every point below; all supporting results are already in the submitted paper unless tagged [NEW].

**W1 (framing / DLinear).** This is the central point and we treat it as such, but one correction changes the conclusion. We appreciate the reviewer holding the method to a from-scratch DLinear, and the observation is exactly right for RR-MoA-proper, the minimal diagnostic probe whose only role is to isolate the router input. We would gently add that it does not carry over to the method we deploy: Residual-IA+, reported in the submitted Appendix P, matches or beats DLinear rather than trailing it:

- 65 significant wins vs 11 losses (5.9:1); 107/123 match-or-beat (87%) across 6 backbones × 6 datasets × 4 horizons.
- 6/6 at the H=192 deployment horizon; MOMENT-large 23/24 with zero losses (16 significant wins); Moirai-MoE 15/15 (100%).
- It dominates on non-stationary data at long horizons (ETTm2 -27.0% at H=720; ETTh2 wins at all four horizons).
- Even at the single least-favorable slice cited (MOMENT-small, H=96), the net mean gap is -2.8%, a win, with ETTh1 the only loss.

The criticism is fair about our framing, not our evidence. We led with "5/6 match-or-beat" and titled the appendix "Closing the DLinear Gap," which put the single losing cell (ETTh1/H=96) front and center. We will fix the presentation in three ways:

- Promote the full grid and the 65:11 win-count into the main text.
- Retitle the section to the outperformance the numbers actually show.
- Reframe the abstract's DLinear comparison as scope rather than deficit, with wording such as: "Because the router isolates the collapse mechanism rather than maximizing accuracy, the minimal RR-MoA probe trails a from-scratch DLinear on linear-dominated datasets; our deployment adapter Residual-IA+ removes this gap, matching or beating DLinear across six backbones and four horizons."

We also accept the narrow, true version of the point: RR-MoA-proper does trail DLinear in absolute MSE, most clearly on ETTh1/H=96. We will introduce it plainly as a diagnostic instrument, not an accuracy claim.

**W2 (Figure 2).** Agreed. We will redraw Figure 2 at larger size with non-overlapping modules and a clearer depiction of the raw-router and frozen-expert paths.

**W3 (Moirai gains without collapse).** A fair distinction. Moirai applies non-learnable instance normalization (Kim et al. 2022, i.e. RevIN) to inputs/outputs, stripping the same per-window location-scale we study, minus the learnable affine. Raw routing recovers the stripped signal there by the same input-side mechanism, while the absence of learnable affine is exactly why AdaMix does not collapse on Moirai: the sudden collapse is driven by gradient co-adaptation and requires a learnable affine. The unified claim is "raw routing helps whenever per-window statistics are stripped from the router's input," and collapse is the severe failure mode that additionally requires learnable affine. We will present the cross-backbone results as consistent with the diagnosis rather than as uniform collapse-repair, and add the Moirai citation.

**W4 (heavy tuning; generalization beyond six).** On "heavy tuning": the 546-run sweep was development effort, and we agree it should not be presented as a SOTA search. We would add that the endpoint is not merely parity with DLinear but a win (65:11), and that the recipe is fixed rather than per-dataset tuned. [NEW] Applied unchanged (gate-init b=-2, 5-epoch warmup, shared NLinear, validation early-stop) to three datasets it had never seen, Residual-IA+ matches or beats DLinear on 8/9 (dataset, seed) cells: Solar 3/3 (-9.5%), Traffic 3/3 (parity), Exchange 2/3, no collapse. A recipe that transfers to unseen data without re-tuning speaks against the dataset-specific-engineering reading, and directly addresses "generalization beyond these six is unclear."

On "the raw branch does the work; the TSFM is dead weight (P.3)": one clarification we should have made explicit. P.3's "dead weight" verdict is measured against the intermediate Dual-Stream (ETTh2 0.452, ETTm2 0.252), not the final Residual-IA+ (ETTh2 0.346, ETTm2 0.188), and that intermediate architecture itself loses to DLinear. P.3's own backbone-free Raw-MLP MoE loses to DLinear by +11.2% on all six datasets: remove the TSFM and you fall behind DLinear; it is the TSFM-inclusive Residual-IA+ that gets ahead. [NEW] We ran the clean isolation directly, Residual-IA+ vs an identical-budget backbone-free Raw-MLP MoE, holding the raw branch fixed and toggling only the backbone, at H=192 (where the paper reports the backbone contributes maximally): Residual-IA+ wins 18/18 (mean -11.8%), including ETTh2/ETTm2/Electricity, the very datasets flagged as dead-weight at H=96, while still matching or beating a 49K DLinear. The backbone's contribution is therefore horizon-dependent: small at H=96 on linear-dominated data, decisively positive at H≥192.

**W5 ((μ,σ) tension).** The tension is real, and re-scoping Observation 1 resolves it: R(D) is the ratio of routing-discriminative variance in the instance-norm-removable component (location-scale) to that in the surviving component (shape), not a claim that (μ,σ) is the whole routing signal. When the ratio is high, stripping (μ,σ) removes most of the routing signal and routing collapses; when it is low (Traffic, R=0.14) the signal lives in the surviving shape, so stripping does not hurt and RR-MoA correctly does not improve. This is exactly consistent with the ablations cited: [μ,σ]-only routing degrades +48% (SSR) and temporal shuffling moves performance ≤3%. We will re-scope Observation 1 explicitly as a vulnerability predictor / lower bound, not a sufficiency claim.

**W6 (minor).** The exact router count is 853 for the reported K=5 model: a Conv1d gate (528 parameters) plus a Linear(64, K) output head (325 at K=5), consistent across the main text, Fig 2, Table A.1, and the released code. Because that head scales with the number of experts K, counting over our expert-count sweep (Table I.2, up to K=10, where the head reaches 650) puts the router in the 1,000-1,200 range at the high end; the Checklist's "~1.1K" reflects that larger-K count rather than the reported K=5 configuration, and we will align it to 853. On the SR-MoA figure, the referent is RR-MoA (SR-MoA improves on RR-MoA across all six datasets, Table F.2), not the baselines.

**Q1 (input length 512 / horizon 96).** The input length is indeed fixed at 512, and the reviewer is right to probe it. Multi-horizon results, though, are already in the submitted paper (Table 14: RR-MoA 12/12 vs best fixed; Residual-IA+ 6/6 at H=192, over H∈{96,192,336,720}); we may not have surfaced them prominently enough. [NEW] For input length we add an ablation (L∈{96,192,336,512}, 6 datasets, 3 seeds): routing never collapses (entropy 0.98-1.48 at every L), raw routing beats the normalized-routing control at all 24 cells, and beats the best fixed adapter at 70/72. Conclusions hold on both axes.

**Q2 (α inconsistency).** Thank you, this is a wording slip. α is initialized at σ(0)=0.5 (the logit is a parameter at 0.0); 0.492 is the mean α at the end of the first logged epoch, after one epoch has moved it below 0.5, not the initialization (trajectory 0.5 → 0.492 → 0.468). We will correct the wording.

**On significance.** The durable contribution is the diagnosis and its predictor, and the reframing above sharpens rather than shrinks it. Normalization-induced routing collapse is a real, mechanistically-explained failure of the standard MoE-adapter upgrade on the dominant instance-normalized TSFM class. R(D) turns that diagnosis into an actionable, training-free tool: computed from raw statistics before any training, it predicts whether raw routing will help on a new dataset (ρ=-0.88 across nine datasets), and equally where it will not (the Traffic null, R=0.14, predicted a priori and confirmed). This go/no-go test transfers beyond our six benchmarks and beyond our specific router, since two architecturally distinct variants (SR-MoA and Residual-IA+) confirm the principle, and it holds regardless of which backbone is best on a given dataset. That, with the raw-routing intervention, is the contribution we ask the reader to take from the paper.

Given the corrected DLinear framing (Residual-IA+ outperforms DLinear 65:11, already in App. P), the re-scoped R(D) account, and the added input-length ablation, together with the reviewer's kind indication that addressing the concerns would raise the score, we would be grateful for a reconsideration of the rating.

W3 now addresses the reviewer's argument head-on and explicitly (9,443 chars, still under 10k, zero hazards). The rewrite does four things the old version left implicit:

1. **Concedes the valid part directly** — "The reviewer is right… on Moirai there is no collapse, so its 12–29% gain is not collapse-repair."
2. **Reframes Moirai as two results** — (1) it *confirms* the mechanism's negative prediction (no learnable affine → no collapse), and (2) raw routing still helps by a *separate* route.
3. **Refutes the P.3/raw-predictiveness link with the architecture** — the key clarification: *"in RR-MoA the raw signal feeds only the router, while the experts consume frozen hidden states and never see the raw input, so the Moirai gain cannot be the Pure Raw-MLP mechanism, whose experts consume the raw signal directly."* The reviewer conflated two different architectures; RR-MoA's Moirai gain is necessarily a routing effect, because raw never reaches the experts.
4. **Concedes point 6 explicitly** — cross-backbone wins presented as *two regimes* (collapse-repair vs routing-signal recovery), "not as uniform validation of the collapse diagnosis."

So it agrees where the reviewer is right (no collapse-repair on Moirai; don't over-claim uniform validation) while cleanly correcting the one conflation (P.3's mechanism needs experts to see raw; RR-MoA's don't). That turns Moirai into a *confirming* negative control plus evidence of broader applicability, rather than a crack in the causal chain.

This is exactly consistent with the ablations cited: [μ,σ]-only routing degrades +48% (SSR) and temporal shuffling moves performance ≤3%. We will re-scope Observation 1 explicitly as a vulnerability predictor / lower bound, not a sufficiency claim.

That, with the raw-routing intervention, is the contribution we ask the reader to take from the paper.

Given the corrected DLinear framing (Residual-IA+ outperforms DLinear 65:11, already in App. P), the re-scoped R(D) account, and the added input-length ablation, together with the reviewer's kind indication that addressing the concerns would raise the score, we would be grateful for a reconsideration of the rating.

**Response to Reviewer Pm4m**

We are grateful for the reviewer's exceptionally close and careful reading: the comments engage the appendix tables and the checklist down to fine details, such as the router parameter count and the α initialization, as attentively as the headline claims, and this is exactly the kind of scrutiny that makes a paper stronger. We also thank the reviewer for noting that addressing these concerns would raise the score. We address every point below; all supporting results are already in the submitted paper unless tagged [NEW].

**W1 (framing / DLinear).** This is the central point and we treat it as such. The reviewer is correct that our abstract's headline numbers (54/54; 12-79% over full fine-tuning) are all comparisons within the frozen-adapter/PEFT regime; those are the right baselines for the frozen-adapter question we ask, and we agree a from-scratch DLinear belongs beside them as an out-of-regime yardstick. That yardstick is exactly right for RR-MoA-proper, the minimal diagnostic probe whose only role is to isolate the router input; we would gently add that it does not carry over to the method we deploy: Residual-IA+, reported in the submitted Appendix P, matches or beats DLinear rather than trailing it:

- 65 significant wins vs 11 losses (5.9:1); 107/123 match-or-beat (87%) across 6 backbones × 6 datasets × 4 horizons.
- 6/6 at the H=192 deployment horizon; MOMENT-large 23/24 with zero losses (16 significant wins); Moirai-MoE 15/15 (100%).
- It dominates on non-stationary data at long horizons (ETTm2 -27.0% at H=720; ETTh2 wins at all four horizons).
- Even at the single least-favorable slice cited (MOMENT-small, H=96), the net mean gap is -2.8%, a win, with ETTh1 the only loss.

The criticism is fair about our framing, not our evidence. We led with "5/6 match-or-beat" and titled the appendix "Closing the DLinear Gap," which put the single losing cell (ETTh1/H=96) front and center. We will fix the presentation in three ways:

- Promote the full grid, the 65:11 win-count, and the backbone-contribution analysis (App. P.3) into the main text, as the reviewer asks.
- Retitle the section to the outperformance the numbers actually show.
- Reframe the abstract's DLinear comparison as scope rather than deficit, with wording such as: "Because the router isolates the collapse mechanism rather than maximizing accuracy, the minimal RR-MoA probe trails a from-scratch DLinear on linear-dominated datasets; our deployment adapter Residual-IA+ removes this gap, matching or beating DLinear across six backbones and four horizons."

We will present RR-MoA-proper plainly as a diagnostic instrument, not an accuracy claim.

**W2 (Figure 2).** Agreed. We will redraw Figure 2 at larger size with non-overlapping modules so it clearly depicts both the raw-router and frozen-expert paths and the paper's core contribution, raw-input routing as the causal fix.

**W3 (Moirai gains without collapse).** The reviewer is right, and we should have drawn this distinction explicitly: on Moirai there is no collapse, so its 12-29% gain is not collapse-repair. We read Moirai as two separate results. (1) It confirms the mechanism's negative prediction: with no learnable-affine input normalization, the gradient co-adaptation that drives collapse cannot occur, and Moirai does not collapse, exactly as the diagnosis requires. (2) Raw routing still helps because Moirai's non-learnable instance normalization (Kim et al. 2022) strips per-window location-scale from the hidden states, so restoring the raw input lets the router recover it. This is a routing effect, not the expert-level raw predictiveness the reviewer links to P.3: in RR-MoA the raw signal feeds only the router, while the experts consume frozen hidden states and never see the raw input, so the Moirai gain cannot be the Pure Raw-MLP mechanism, whose experts consume the raw signal directly. We therefore agree the cross-backbone wins should be presented as two regimes, collapse-repair on learnable-affine RevIN backbones and routing-signal recovery elsewhere, not as uniform validation of the collapse diagnosis, and we will add the Moirai citation.

**W4 (heavy tuning; generalization beyond six).** On "heavy tuning": the 546-run sweep was development effort, and we agree it should not be presented as a SOTA search. We would add that the endpoint is not merely parity with DLinear but a win (65:11), and that the recipe is fixed rather than per-dataset tuned. [NEW] Applied unchanged (gate-init b=-2, 5-epoch warmup, shared NLinear, validation early-stop) to three datasets it had never seen, Residual-IA+ matches or beats DLinear on 8/9 (dataset, seed) cells: Solar 3/3 (-9.5%), Traffic 3/3 (parity), Exchange 2/3, no collapse. A recipe that transfers to unseen data without re-tuning speaks against the dataset-specific-engineering reading, and directly addresses "generalization beyond these six is unclear."

On "the raw branch does the work; the TSFM is dead weight (P.3)": one clarification we should have made explicit. P.3's "dead weight" verdict is measured against the intermediate Dual-Stream (ETTh2 0.452, ETTm2 0.252), not the final Residual-IA+ (ETTh2 0.346, ETTm2 0.188), and that intermediate architecture itself loses to DLinear. P.3's own backbone-free Raw-MLP MoE loses to DLinear by +11.2% on all six datasets: remove the TSFM and you fall behind DLinear; it is the TSFM-inclusive Residual-IA+ that gets ahead. [NEW] We ran the clean isolation directly, Residual-IA+ vs an identical-budget backbone-free Raw-MLP MoE, holding the raw branch fixed and toggling only the backbone, at H=192 (where the paper reports the backbone contributes maximally): Residual-IA+ wins 18/18 (mean -11.8%), including ETTh2/ETTm2/Electricity, the very datasets flagged as dead-weight at H=96, while still matching or beating a 49K DLinear. The backbone's contribution is therefore horizon-dependent: small at H=96 on linear-dominated data, decisively positive at H≥192.

**W5 ((μ,σ) tension).** The tension is real, and re-scoping Observation 1 resolves it: R(D) is the ratio of routing-discriminative variance in the instance-norm-removable component (location-scale) to that in the surviving component (shape), not a claim that (μ,σ) is the whole routing signal. When the ratio is high, stripping (μ,σ) removes most of the routing signal and routing collapses; when it is low (Traffic, R=0.14) the signal lives in the surviving shape, so stripping does not hurt and RR-MoA correctly does not improve. This is exactly consistent with the ablations cited: [μ,σ]-only routing degrades +48% (SSR) and temporal shuffling moves performance ≤3%. We agree the operative routing signal is broader than (μ,σ): it includes the order-invariant shape that survives normalization, which is precisely R(D)'s surviving component. We will re-scope Observation 1 explicitly as a vulnerability predictor / lower bound, not a sufficiency claim.

**W6 (minor).** The exact router count is 853 for the reported K=5 model: a Conv1d gate (528 parameters) plus a Linear(64, K) output head (325 at K=5), consistent across the main text, Fig 2, Table A.1, and the released code. Because that head scales with the number of experts K, counting over our expert-count sweep (Table I.2, up to K=10, where the head reaches 650) puts the router in the 1,000-1,200 range at the high end; the Checklist's "~1.1K" reflects that larger-K count rather than the reported K=5 configuration, and we will align it to 853. On the SR-MoA figure, the referent is RR-MoA (SR-MoA improves on RR-MoA across all six datasets, Table F.2), not the baselines. We will also standardize "fine-tuning" throughout and double-check the R(D) parenthesis the reviewer flagged.

**Q1 (input length 512 / horizon 96).** The input length is indeed fixed at 512, and the reviewer is right to probe it. Multi-horizon results, though, are already in the submitted paper (Table 14: RR-MoA 12/12 vs best fixed; Residual-IA+ 6/6 at H=192, over H∈{96,192,336,720}); we may not have surfaced them prominently enough. [NEW] For input length we add an ablation (L∈{96,192,336,512}, 6 datasets, 3 seeds): routing never collapses (entropy 0.98-1.48 at every L), raw routing beats the normalized-routing control at all 24 cells, and beats the best fixed adapter at 70/72. Conclusions hold on both axes.

**Q2 (α inconsistency).** Thank you, this is a wording slip. α is initialized at σ(0)=0.5 (the logit is a parameter at 0.0); 0.492 is the mean α at the end of the first logged epoch, after one epoch has moved it below 0.5, not the initialization (trajectory 0.5 → 0.492 → 0.468). We will correct the wording.

**On significance.** The durable contribution is the diagnosis and its predictor, and the reframing above sharpens rather than shrinks it. Normalization-induced routing collapse is a real, mechanistically-explained failure of the standard MoE-adapter upgrade on the dominant instance-normalized TSFM class. R(D) turns that diagnosis into an actionable, training-free tool: computed from raw statistics before any training, it predicts whether raw routing will help on a new dataset (ρ=-0.88 across nine datasets), and equally where it will not (the Traffic null, R=0.14, predicted a priori and confirmed). This go/no-go test transfers beyond our six benchmarks and beyond our specific router, since two architecturally distinct variants (SR-MoA and Residual-IA+) confirm the principle, and it holds regardless of which backbone is best on a given dataset. That, with the raw-routing intervention, is the contribution we ask the reader to take from the paper.

Given the corrected DLinear framing (Residual-IA+ outperforms DLinear 65:11, already in App. P), the re-scoped R(D) account, and the added input-length ablation, together with the reviewer's kind indication that addressing the concerns would raise the score, we would be grateful for a reconsideration of the rating.
